name: GURPS Fourth Edition
author: GM Toolkit
description: Generic Universal RolePlaying System, Fourth Edition: no class, no level, no fixed skill list. Every capability comes from how a shared character-point budget is spent across four point-bought primary attributes, secondary characteristics derived from them (with an independent buy-up/buy-down adjustment for each, per GURPS's own rules), an open-ended list of advantages/disadvantages/quirks, and an open-ended list of individually-bought skills -- both repeating groups with no enum of valid entries, since GURPS has hundreds of each. This is the schema format's genericity acid test: SYSTEMS.md's GURPS worked sketch is reproduced here in full, plus additional real GURPS 4e Basic Set derived values (Dodge, Basic Lift) added specifically to exercise the formula evaluator further -- multi-hop dependency chains, a field multiplied by itself, and this profile's only use of `rounding: ceiling`.

pcFields.label: ST (Strength)
pcFields.helpText: Physical power and lifting/striking ability. Point-bought like every GURPS attribute -- there is no class or level anywhere in this profile; a character's capabilities come entirely from how points are spent across attributes, secondary characteristics, advantages/disadvantages, and skills below.

pcFields.label: DX (Dexterity)
pcFields.helpText: Agility, coordination, and fine motor control.

pcFields.label: IQ (Intelligence)
pcFields.helpText: Reasoning ability and mental acuity.

pcFields.label: HT (Health)
pcFields.helpText: Physical vitality, resistance to disease/toxin, and stamina.

pcFields.label: ST Point Cost
pcFields.helpText: GURPS 4e Basic Set: ST costs 10 character points per level above 10, and refunds 10 points per level below 10 -- linear in both directions, so the point cost of the score bought is derived directly from the score rather than tracked as a separate player-entered value (issue #87's 'derive point cost from the attribute value if possible').

pcFields.label: DX Point Cost
pcFields.helpText: 20 points per level above 10, -20 per level below 10.

pcFields.label: IQ Point Cost
pcFields.helpText: 20 points per level above 10, -20 per level below 10.

pcFields.label: HT Point Cost
pcFields.helpText: 10 points per level above 10, -10 per level below 10.

pcFields.label: Attribute Points Spent
pcFields.helpText: Total character points spent across the four primary attributes -- a derived field chained off the four cost fields above, itself proving the evaluator handles multi-hop dependency chains (attributePointsSpent -> stCost -> st), not just single-hop references to a flat attribute.

pcFields.label: HP Adjustment
pcFields.helpText: GURPS lets a character buy Hit Points up or down independently of ST, at 2 character points per +1/-1 HP. Defaults to 0 (HP exactly equal to ST) until points are spent here.

pcFields.label: HP Point Cost
pcFields.helpText: 2 character points per HP bought above (or refunded per HP below) the ST-derived default.

pcFields.label: Will Point Cost
pcFields.helpText: 5 character points per level.

pcFields.label: Perception Point Cost
pcFields.helpText: 5 character points per level, same rate as Will.

pcFields.label: FP Point Cost
pcFields.helpText: 3 character points per level.

pcFields.label: Basic Speed
pcFields.helpText: (HT + DX) / 4, plus any points spent adjusting it -- GURPS's actual Basic Speed formula. Genuinely needs the fractional remainder (5.25, not 5), which is exactly why the grammar's `/` is ordinary real-valued division rather than floor/integer division (SYSTEMS.md's 'Rounding is field metadata').

pcFields.label: Basic Speed Point Cost
pcFields.helpText: 20 character points per full +1 to Basic Speed (equivalently 5 points per the usual +0.25 increment); speedAdjustment moves in whole numbers in this profile, so the cost scales at the same 20-per-level rate.

pcFields.label: Basic Move
pcFields.helpText: floor(Basic Speed), plus any points spent adjusting it directly -- referencing basicSpeed (itself a derived field) proves formula chaining works, not just single-hop references to a flat attribute (SYSTEMS.md's GURPS sketch).

pcFields.label: Basic Move Point Cost
pcFields.helpText: 5 character points per level.

pcFields.label: Dodge Adjustment
pcFields.helpText: Enhanced Dodge and similar traits add a flat bonus here rather than the formula branching on which trait is present.

pcFields.label: Dodge
pcFields.helpText: GURPS 4e's actual Dodge formula: floor(Basic Speed) + 3. Deliberately references basicSpeed directly rather than basicMove -- Dodge is defined off Basic Speed's own whole number, not off however much Basic Move was separately bought, so basicMove's moveAdjustment must not leak into this value.

pcFields.label: Basic Lift
pcFields.helpText: GURPS 4e's actual Basic Lift formula: ST squared, divided by 5, rounded up. Demonstrates the grammar multiplying a field by itself (no exponent syntax needed -- `st * st` is ordinary multiplication), and this profile's only use of `rounding: ceiling` (every derived field elsewhere in the four built-in profiles rounds down).

pcFields.label: Thrust Damage
pcFields.helpText: GURPS 4e's Thrust damage for this ST, read off the (non-linear) ST-to-damage table on Basic Set p.16 -- e.g. '1d-2' at ST 10, '2d+1' at ST 19. Unlike basicLift above, this genuinely can't be a `derived` formula: the table's steps aren't a fixed linear function of ST (nor any single fixed shape at all), so expressing it would need a lookup, and the grammar has no lookup/branching facility by design (SYSTEMS.md's 'Explicitly disallowed' section). Entered directly, same resolution as GURPS skill level below.

pcFields.label: Swing Damage
pcFields.helpText: GURPS 4e's Swing damage for this ST, from the same non-linear table as Thrust Damage above -- e.g. '1d' at ST 10, '3d+2' at ST 19.

pcFields.label: Tech Level (TL)
pcFields.helpText: GURPS's genre/technology-era concept -- not the same thing as a D&D 'Level' despite the similar-looking name; it gates which equipment/skills exist for this setting (TL3 muskets vs. TL7 rifles vs. TL10 blasters) and several skills default off it. TL0 (Stone Age) through TL12 (roughly a century past today) per the Basic Set.

pcFields.label: Advantages, Disadvantages & Quirks
pcFields.helpText: Open-ended list, player-chosen -- GURPS has hundreds of published advantages and disadvantages, plus homebrew ones, so there is deliberately no enum of valid names here (only Category below is a closed list, and it names the four kinds of trait GURPS itself recognizes, not which specific traits are allowed).

pcFields.label: Skills
pcFields.helpText: Individually-bought skills, open-ended -- GURPS has 100+ published skills, many with specialties (e.g. 'Guns (Pistol)'), so Name is free text rather than an enum. Skill Level and Points are directly-entered numbers, not `derived` fields, for two independent reasons the RFC (SYSTEMS.md) found doing GURPS first: (1) Controlling Attribute varies per row -- 'add whichever of ST/DX/IQ/HT this row names' is dynamic dispatch on a field's own value, which the grammar structurally can't express (same limit that keeps D&D saves/skills and Pathfinder's proficiency rank flat too); (2) GURPS's real points-to-level conversion is a difficulty-based lookup table (Easy/Average/Hard/Very Hard, non-linear in points spent), not arithmetic at all -- a second, independent reason a formula couldn't reach it even if (1) didn't already rule it out.

npcFields.label: ST (Strength)
npcFields.helpText: GURPS has no separate monster-stat-block format -- an NPC is built exactly like a PC, with the same point-bought attributes, secondary characteristics, traits, and skills below.

npcFields.label: Reaction to PCs
npcFields.helpText: GM-facing: this NPC's starting attitude toward the party, per GURPS 4e's own Reaction Rolls table categories (Basic Set p.494) -- informs (not dictates) how the GM plays them at the table. Absent from the PC side of this pack; a PC has no need to track its own reaction to itself.

npcFields.label: GM Notes
npcFields.helpText: GM-only notes -- motivations, secrets, plot hooks. Not shown to players; that's a display-layer concern the schema itself doesn't enforce.
